title: LLMs & Applied AI Engineering
summary: An LLM is a very good next-token guesser wrapped in a product. Knowing the few moving parts — tokens, context, RAG, agents, cost — is what separates calling an API from defending a real system.

blocks.markdown:
An LLM is a neural net that predicts the **next token** — everything else is that, repeated.

- Chat, code, and summaries are all repeated **next-token prediction**.
- It learned patterns from huge text into frozen **weights** — it has no live knowledge.
- That is exactly why it can be **confidently wrong**.
- The AI engineer's job is steering it: prompting, grounding, tools, cost.

blocks.subTitle: Which tool for the job
blocks.markdown:
Pick the technique by what you actually need.

| Need | Reach for |
|---|---|
| Quick tweak, prototype | Prompting |
| Private or changing facts | RAG |
| Consistent tone/format | Fine-tuning |
| Live data or actions | Agent + tools |
| Find similar things | Embeddings + vector DB |

blocks.subTitle: Tokens
blocks.markdown:
Text is chopped into **tokens** — word-pieces, not whole words.

- Rule of thumb: 1 token ≈ **4 characters ≈ 0.75 words**, so 1,000 tokens ≈ 750 words.
- Rare or long words split into several tokens ("unhappiness" → un, happ, iness).
- This matters because you **pay per token** and the context window is counted in tokens.

blocks.subTitle: Transformer & attention
blocks.markdown:
Tokens become **embeddings**, flow through stacked **attention** layers, then the model emits a probability for the next token.

![Transformer flow from tokens to next-token probabilities](assets/llms-applied-ai/transformer-highlevel.svg)

- **Attention** weighs how much each token should focus on every other token.
- It is **parallel**, unlike serial RNNs — which is why transformers scale to big hardware.
- Cost: every token compares to every other, so compute grows ~**O(n²)** with length.

assets.alt: Transformer flow from tokens to next-token probabilities

blocks.subTitle: Context window & temperature
blocks.markdown:
The **context window** is the max tokens — input plus output — the model can attend to at once.

- Anything outside the window is **invisible**; sizes range ~8K to 1M tokens.
- Each call is **stateless** — chat "memory" is just the prior turns re-sent every time.
- **Temperature** controls randomness: 0 = deterministic and most-likely; higher = more variety.

blocks.subTitle: Embeddings
blocks.markdown:
An **embedding** is a vector of numbers that captures meaning — similar meanings sit close together.

- Compare them with **cosine similarity** / nearest-neighbor search.
- Powers **semantic search**, clustering, dedup, and the "retrieve" step of RAG.
- Vectors are typically **384–3072** dimensions, stored in a vector DB.

blocks.subTitle: RAG in five steps
blocks.markdown:
**RAG** = retrieve real text, paste it into the prompt, then answer grounded in it.

![RAG pipeline: query, embed, retrieve, augment, generate](assets/llms-applied-ai/rag-pipeline.svg)

- Embed the query → search the vector DB → take **top-k** chunks → build the prompt → generate.
- Instruct the model to answer **only from context** and say "I don't know" otherwise.
- It cuts **hallucination** by making the model a reader of supplied facts, not a recaller.

assets.alt: RAG pipeline: query, embed, retrieve, augment, generate

blocks.subTitle: Agents & tool use
blocks.markdown:
An **agent** is an LLM in a loop: think → call a tool → observe → repeat until done.

![The agent think, call, observe loop](assets/llms-applied-ai/agent-loop.svg)

- **Function calling** lets the model return structured arguments for a tool you describe.
- Your code runs the tool and feeds the result back; the **model stays stateless**.
- This turns a passive text generator into something that takes actions and uses live data.

assets.alt: The agent think, call, observe loop

blocks.subTitle: RAG vs fine-tuning vs prompting
blocks.markdown:
They solve different problems — and they compose.

| Technique | Best for |
|---|---|
| Prompting | Instant tweaks, prototypes |
| RAG | Private or changing facts |
| Fine-tuning | Consistent style/format |

- Fine-tuning teaches **behavior, not fresh facts** — never use it to add knowledge.
- For current or private facts, prefer **RAG**; it grounds and lets you cite sources.
- You can fine-tune for format **and** use RAG for facts in one app.

blocks.subTitle: Cost & latency levers
blocks.markdown:
You trade on cost and latency every request.

- **Billing** is per input + output token — bigger model, longer prompt, longer answer all cost more.
- **Latency scales with output length**: generation is serial, one token at a time.
- Long prompts mainly raise **time-to-first-token (TTFT)**.
- Cut both: smaller model, shorter outputs, cache repeats and embeddings, retrieve fewer/better chunks.

blocks.subTitle: Real systems
blocks.markdown:
The patterns you meet in production:

- **Support bots** index docs in a vector DB and retrieve top chunks — they rarely fine-tune, since docs change weekly ([caching](caching)).
- **GitHub Copilot** is latency-critical: the work is assembling the right code context fast and keeping TTFT low.
- **Vector DBs** (Pinecone, pgvector, FAISS) use **ANN** indexes like HNSW — trading slight recall for huge speed.
- **Frontier APIs** expose function calling so your app owns the loop and tools.

blocks.subTitle: Signals to watch
blocks.markdown:
An LLM app is an operational system — watch these:

- **TTFT and tokens/sec** (p50/p95/p99): rising TTFT means overload or prompts too long.
- **Cost per request**: a creeping average means growing prompts or a pricier model.
- **Retrieval quality (recall@k)**: many low-similarity hits mean RAG is degrading silently.
- **Refusal rate**: too high = retrieval failing; too low = possible hallucination.

The mistakes that bite in interviews and production:

- **"It knows current facts."** Weights froze at a cutoff — supply recent/private facts via RAG or tools.
- **"Fine-tune to add knowledge."** It shapes style, not facts, and can't stay fresh — use RAG.
- **"Bigger window, paste everything."** Long prompts cost more and bury the answer ("lost in the middle").
- **"Temperature 0 makes it correct."** It only makes it deterministic, not true.
- **Prompt injection**: untrusted text smuggles instructions — filter inputs, use least-privilege tools.
- **"One demo means it works."** Without an eval set, a prompt change can quietly break 10% of cases.
